subsection: 11. Cultural nationalism, the churches and social change, and developments in science

notes.h: Romanticism: a reaction against the Enlightenment
notes.b: Romanticism was a cultural movement that put feeling, imagination, nature, the individual and the national past above reason and classical rules. It grew up as a reaction against the Enlightenment, and it gave nationalists their raw material.
points: The Enlightenment of the eighteenth century valued reason, order, universal rules and classical models in art. Romantic writers and artists rejected this rational order in favour of feeling, imagination and the national past.

The German thinker Johann Gottfried Herder (1744-1803) wrote in the late eighteenth century that each people has its own spirit, expressed in its language, folk songs and customs. This idea of a national spirit was later called the Volksgeist, and nationalists took it up.
Folklore collection and the revival of medieval legends were central to cultural nationalism, since they claimed to reveal the true character of a people, one older than any government or frontier.
Victor Hugo's preface to his play Cromwell (1827) served as a manifesto for Romantic drama, in other words a public statement of what the new drama should be, free of classical rules.

Romanticism was an artistic movement, not a political programme, so Romantics could be conservative or revolutionary. The early Hugo was a royalist, whereas Richard Wagner took part in a rising in 1849.
notes.tip: Define Romanticism by what it rejected (reason and classical rules) and what it valued (feeling, nature, the national past). Do not confuse it with liberalism and nationalism, which are political ideas.

notes.h: Cultural nationalism and peoples without a state
notes.b: Nationalism is the belief that a people sharing language, culture and history forms a nation that should rule itself. Cultural nationalism uses music, art, literature, history and language to express and build that sense of nationhood, often before any political state exists.
points: The Vienna settlement of 1815 drew frontiers by dynasty and the balance of power, not by nationality. Italians, Germans, Poles, Czechs and Hungarians were therefore divided or ruled by others, which is why culture mattered so much to peoples without a state.

Cultural nationalism was strongest where a nation lacked its own state, as among Italians, Germans, Poles, Czechs, Hungarians and Finns. With no government of their own to express nationhood, they used songs, stories, paintings and language instead.
Cultural nationalism fed political nationalism: once people felt they shared a past, a language and symbols, it was a short step to demanding a state to match, as later happened in Italy and Germany.
Artists and composers often worked with patrons and publishers in national capitals, and their audiences helped to shape national identity by sharing the same songs, stories and images.
Nationalists treated language as the main mark of nationality, so scholars and writers who collected, wrote and standardised a language were building a nation as well as a literature.
notes.tip: For 'how far did culture contribute to nationalism' essays, a judgement is needed: it was strongest where there was no state, it reached the educated more than the masses, and it prepared political unity rather than achieving it.

notes.h: Music and national identity: Chopin, Liszt and Verdi
notes.b: Music could speak for a nation without words, so it escaped censors and reached people who could not read. Three composers show how folk rhythms and opera plots became symbols of Poland, Hungary and Italy.
points: Frederic Chopin (1810-1849) wrote mazurkas and polonaises, which are Polish dance forms. He left Warsaw in 1830, and the Polish November Rising of 1830-31 was crushed by Russia, so he settled in Paris in 1831.

Because Chopin lived in exile in Paris, his music became a voice of Polish national feeling. Robert Schumann wrote that Chopin's works were 'cannons buried in flowers', meaning that patriotic force was hidden inside delicate music.

Franz Liszt (1811-1886), born in the Kingdom of Hungary, wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies, most of them about 1846-53. They used what he took to be Hungarian folk music, much of it in fact Romani, and presented Hungary to European audiences.

Giuseppe Verdi (1813-1901) staged Nabucco in Milan (La Scala) in 1842. Its chorus of Hebrew slaves, 'Va, pensiero', came to be heard as patriotic by Italians who felt themselves oppressed, though the patriotic reading grew later rather than at the premiere.

Around 1859 the cry 'Viva VERDI' was a coded political slogan, because the letters stood for Vittorio Emanuele Re d'Italia, the king the nationalists wanted. It let crowds shout for unification under the eyes of the authorities.
Verdi's standing as a patriotic figure was confirmed when he was elected a deputy to the first Italian parliament in 1861.
notes.tip: Say that Va, pensiero 'came to be heard' as patriotic; do not claim it was a political call at its 1842 premiere. The 'Viva VERDI' slogan of about 1859 is safe. Explain how each work built national feeling, not the composer's life.

notes.h: Music and national identity: Wagner, Smetana and Glinka
notes.b: German, Czech and Russian composers drew on national myth, folk song and history to create national opera. Some of their best-known works came only after 1871, so dates matter.
points: Richard Wagner (1813-1883) used German myth and legend in his operas, such as Tannhauser (1845) and Lohengrin (1850), so that audiences met a shared German legendary past on stage.

Wagner's Ring cycle is based on the Nibelungenlied (a medieval German epic) and Norse sagas. It was first performed complete at Bayreuth in 1876, after the period 1815-1871, so it should not be presented as an achievement within it.
Wagner took part in the Dresden rising of May 1849 and fled to Switzerland, which shows that Romantic artists could be revolutionary as well as nationalist.

Bedrich Smetana (1824-1884) wrote the Czech national opera The Bartered Bride, first performed in Prague in 1866. It used Czech folk music, so Czech audiences heard their own culture on the opera stage.
Smetana's cycle of symphonic poems Ma vlast (1874-79), which includes Vltava, drew on Czech landscape and history, but it also came after 1871.
Mikhail Glinka's A Life for the Tsar (1836) is seen as the start of Russian national opera.
notes.tip: Prefer Wagner's earlier operas and The Bartered Bride (1866) as evidence from within the period. If you mention the Ring or Ma vlast, say they came after 1871.

notes.h: Art and national identity: Delacroix, Friedrich and history painting
notes.b: Painters gave nations visible symbols. A single image such as a flag, a landscape or a scene from the past could make a shared identity feel real to people who could not read a pamphlet.
points: Eugene Delacroix (1798-1863) painted Liberty Leading the People in 1830, after the July Revolution. It shows Liberty carrying the tricolour (the French flag) and leading Parisians of different classes over a barricade, so it became a symbol of liberty and of the French nation.
The painting was shown at the Paris Salon in 1831 and bought by the French state, which shows how far a revolutionary image had become part of the official picture of France.
Delacroix's Massacre at Chios (1824) showed sympathy for the Greek cause, a cultural response to the Greek revolt rather than an account of it.
Caspar David Friedrich (1774-1840) painted landscapes such as Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (about 1818). They expressed the Romantic feeling for nature, which was linked to German national feeling.
Romantic history painting showed scenes from the national past, which gave citizens a shared image of their history.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People (1830, France) with his Massacre at Chios (1824, Greece). Name the work and say what symbol it gave the nation.

notes.h: Literature and national identity
notes.b: Writers could make a nation's past and language famous across Europe. These authors worked in different countries, often in exile, and each gave their people a shared story.
points: Jacob (1785-1863) and Wilhelm (1786-1859) Grimm published Children's and Household Tales in 1812 and 1815, which presented German folklore as the voice of the German people.
Jacob Grimm's German Grammar (first volume 1819) and the German Dictionary, begun by the brothers in 1838, treated the language itself as the nation's inheritance.

Alessandro Manzoni (1785-1873) published The Betrothed (I promessi sposi) in 1827. It is set in Lombardy under Spanish rule in the seventeenth century, which readers took as a comment on Austrian rule in their own day.
Manzoni revised the novel in 1840-42 into the educated Italian of Florence (Tuscan), and it became a model for standard Italian.

Adam Mickiewicz (1798-1855) wrote Pan Tadeusz, the Polish national epic, in exile. Published in Paris in 1834 and set in Lithuania in 1811-12, it celebrated the Polish national past at a time when Poland had no state.
Alexander Pushkin (1799-1837), author of Eugene Onegin (complete edition 1833), created the modern Russian literary language, and his works became a central part of Russian national culture.
Sandor Petofi's 'National Song', recited in Pest on 15 March 1848, shows literature acting directly in revolution.
notes.tip: Name each author with the work and date, and say how it built national feeling (folk sources, a national epic, a standard language). Do not confuse the Grimms' tales (1812, 1815), Jacob's Grammar (1819) and their Dictionary (begun 1838).

notes.h: Standardising national languages
notes.b: A nation of people who speak many dialects is hard to imagine as one community. Standard languages, taught in schools and fixed in books, turned dialects into national languages.
points: Grammars, dictionaries and schools turned dialects into national languages and built a single community of readers, which helped create a sense of one national community. Italian and Czech are examples.
Josef Jungmann's Czech-German dictionary, produced in the 1830s, gave Czech the vocabulary of a literary language at a time when German dominated educated life in the Czech lands.
Elias Lonnrot's Kalevala (1835, enlarged 1849) was a Finnish epic put together from folk poetry. It gave Finns a national story in their own language.
Manzoni's revised Betrothed (1840-42) set Florentine Italian as a model, so a single written Italian could be learnt by readers from different regions.
notes.tip: Examiners reward linking language to nationhood. For each example, say what was standardised (grammar, dictionary, epic) and how it created a community of readers.

notes.h: Key personality: Victor Hugo (literary role)
notes.b: Hugo's literary work made him the leader of French Romanticism and one of the most celebrated writers of the century. Here the focus is on what he wrote and how people judged it.
points: Victor Hugo was born on 26 February 1802 at Besancon, the son of a general under Napoleon. He became a poet, dramatist and novelist and the leader of French Romanticism.

His early works include Odes (1822), Les Orientales (1829), with poems for the Greek cause, the preface to Cromwell (1827) and the play Hernani, first performed at the Comedie-Francaise in February 1830.
Hernani provoked a riot, 'the battle of Hernani', between Romantic supporters and classical critics, and it marked the victory of Romanticism in French theatre.

His novel Notre-Dame de Paris (1831) revived interest in the Gothic past of Paris, so it helped the campaign to preserve and restore medieval buildings. He was elected to the Academie francaise in 1841 and made a peer of France in 1845.

In exile he lived on Jersey (1852-55) and then on Guernsey (1855-70) at Hauteville House. There he wrote Les Contemplations (1856), partly mourning his daughter Leopoldine, who drowned in 1843, and The Toilers of the Sea (1866), set on Guernsey.

Les Misérables (1862), written largely on Guernsey, follows the convict Jean Valjean from 1815 to the Paris rising of June 1832. It deals with poverty, injustice, the law and redemption, and it was a huge success across Europe.

As a writer Hugo shaped taste and national memory, so he was an active participant in cultural life, and his social novels gave a voice to the poor. Romantics hailed him as their leader, while classical critics attacked him for breaking the rules of form and taste.

Some critics found Les Misérables sentimental, but readers made it a best-seller. Historians now rank him among the greatest French writers, a national figure whose literary and political engagement went together, and his state funeral in 1885 and burial in the Panthéon show his standing.
notes.tip: Learn the order of his works: preface to Cromwell (1827), Hernani (1830), Notre-Dame de Paris (1831, before exile), Les Contemplations (1856, poems), Les Misérables (1862, written in exile). Do not mix them up.

notes.h: France: the Catholic revival and the Church's answer to poverty
notes.b: The French Revolution had attacked the Catholic Church, but after 1815 the Church recovered. Its revival split between conservatives, liberal Catholics and lay charity workers, who each responded to the changes of the age.
points: The Revolution seized Church lands and persecuted the clergy, and Napoleon's Concordat (agreement with the Pope, 1801) restored the Church under state control. The Church was therefore linked with monarchy and order, and republicans and liberals were often anticlerical (hostile to the Church's power).

The Catholic revival after 1815 was favoured by the restored Bourbons (1814/15-1830), who stood for 'throne and altar'. New and returning religious orders appeared, and the Church was strong among women, peasants and some regions, but weak among urban workers and much of the middle class.

Liberal Catholicism was led by Felicite de Lamennais, Henri Lacordaire and Charles de Montalembert. Their newspaper L'Avenir (1830, motto 'God and liberty') demanded freedom of the Church from the state, and freedom of the press, education and association.

Pope Gregory XVI condemned these ideas in the encyclical (papal letter) Mirari vos in 1832. Lamennais left the Church in 1834 after his Words of a Believer, whereas Lacordaire and Montalembert submitted and stayed.

Frederic Ozanam (1813-1853), a Catholic student and later a Sorbonne professor, co-founded the Society of St Vincent de Paul in Paris in 1833 with fellow students. It was a lay Catholic charity that visited the poor and the sick in their homes.

The Society spread through France and abroad. It was a Catholic answer to urban poverty and to the charge that the Church ignored the poor. It was named after the seventeenth-century saint, not founded by him.
notes.tip: Say Ozanam co-founded the Society with fellow students. Keep Lamennais (left the Church in 1834) apart from Lacordaire and Montalembert (stayed), and Mirari vos (1832) apart from the Syllabus of Errors (1864).

notes.h: France: schools, pilgrimage, the Pope and anticlericalism
notes.b: From 1850 the French Church gained schools and mass devotion, but its close ties to conservatism and to Pius IX pushed liberals, republicans and many workers away from it.
points: The Falloux Law (March 1850, named after the education minister Alfred de Falloux) gave freedom to open mainly Catholic secondary schools and put clergy on education councils. It greatly expanded Church schooling and was part of the conservative reaction after 1848.

Napoleon III supported the Church until 1859, and French troops protected the Pope in Rome from 1849 to 1870 (withdrawn briefly 1866-67). Italian unification, which threatened the Pope's rule in Rome, strained this relationship.
Popular piety grew too. After Bernadette Soubirous's visions at Lourdes in 1858, mass pilgrimage developed, helped by railways, which could carry large crowds to the shrine.

Ultramontanism means looking to the Pope in Rome for authority. Under Pius IX (1846-78) it grew: he defined the Immaculate Conception (Mary's freedom from sin) as doctrine in 1854 and issued the Syllabus of Errors in 1864, condemning liberalism and progress.

This deepened the split between the Church and liberals, republicans and workers. Anticlericalism and the de-Christianisation of the urban working class followed, and Ernest Renan's Life of Jesus (1863) is an example of the challenge from scholarship.
notes.tip: Keep to the Falloux Law's effect on Church schooling. In 'churches and social change' essays, link each development to a problem (ignorance, poverty) and include the loss of the urban working class.

notes.h: Britain: Nonconformity, Methodism and the Oxford Movement
notes.b: Britain had one established Church but many denominations. Industrial growth created crowded towns where the parish system and old charity broke down, and the churches competed and cooperated in responding.
points: The Church of England was the established (state) Church. Nonconformists such as Methodists, Baptists and Congregationalists stood outside it, and Catholics were a minority, many of them Irish.
Industrialisation and rapid town growth produced crowded towns where the parish system and old charity broke down. This is the social change the churches had to meet.

Methodism, from John Wesley (1703-1791), grew rapidly among industrial workers and miners. Its chapels, preaching, self-improvement and discipline suited working people, and it was also a training ground for trade-union and Chartist speakers.

The Oxford Movement began with John Keble's Assize Sermon in Oxford on 14 July 1833. Its Tracts for the Times (1833-41) gave its followers the name Tractarians, and it revived Catholic worship and ritual within the Church of England.
John Henry Newman became a Catholic in 1845. Later Anglo-Catholic priests worked in slum parishes.

Catholics gained the Catholic Emancipation Act in 1829. Irish immigration to the industrial cities followed, and the Catholic hierarchy was restored in England and Wales in 1850 under Cardinal Wiseman.
notes.tip: Keep the groups apart: Methodism (Wesley, Nonconformist, workers), the Oxford Movement (Keble and Newman, High Church Anglican, ritual), Christian Socialism (Maurice and Kingsley) and Evangelicals (Shaftesbury).

notes.h: Britain: Christian Socialism, schools, temperance and evangelical reform
notes.b: Many British Christians tried to answer poverty, ignorance and drink directly. They set up schools, societies and missions, often run by churches and charities rather than by the state.
points: Christian Socialism, from 1848, was led by F. D. Maurice, Charles Kingsley and J. M. Ludlow. They sought to apply Christian principles to the problems of industrial society and set up co-operative workshops.
The Working Men's College opened in London in 1854, and Kingsley's novel Alton Locke (1850) drew attention to the conditions of workers.

Sunday schools, begun in the late eighteenth century (Robert Raikes), and the ragged schools (the Ragged School Union, 1844) taught poor children. Along with church day schools they were run mainly by churches and charities, because the churches had a central role in schooling before state education.

Temperance societies campaigned against drunkenness, which was seen as a cause of poverty and family breakdown among the working class. The Preston teetotal pledge of 1832 (Joseph Livesey) helped to launch the cause, and many societies were chapel-based.

Evangelical Christians (those stressing personal faith and moral action) such as Lord Shaftesbury, called Lord Ashley until 1851, led campaigns for factory and mines reform, including the Mines Act of 1842.
George Williams founded the YMCA in London in 1844, and churches in the industrial towns ran city missions and charitable work, which responded to urban poverty with preaching, relief and education.
notes.tip: Link each movement to the problem it tackled: drink and temperance, ignorance and Sunday and ragged schools, poverty and Christian Socialism, factory conditions and Shaftesbury.

notes.h: Britain: the 1851 census, the Salvation Army and a comparison with France
notes.b: The churches' efforts had limits, and a census showed that many working people stayed away. The experience of Britain and France differed because of how each country organised religion.
points: The religious census of 1851 (England and Wales) showed that many working people, especially in the big towns, did not attend any church. Do not quote attendance figures, because sources differ widely.
William Booth began his East London mission in 1865, and it was renamed the Salvation Army in 1878. It aimed to reach poor people who did not go to church.

In France there was one Church, tied to conservatism and opposed by anticlericals. In Britain there were many denominations, with Nonconformists linked to reform and self-help, so religion and political reform were less sharply opposed there.
In both countries the churches lost much of the urban working class, so the churches' social work treated symptoms (poverty, drink, ignorance) more than the causes.
notes.tip: Essays on France and Britain need both countries roughly equally, with a judgement of achievements vs limits. The 1851 census is the key evidence for the limits; give no figures.

notes.h: Electricity: Faraday, Maxwell and Siemens
notes.b: Electricity moved from laboratory experiments to a source of power in a few decades. Each scientist here built on the one before.
points: Michael Faraday (1791-1867), working at the Royal Institution in London, showed electromagnetic rotation in 1821. This is the principle of the electric motor, in which electricity makes a magnet and a wire turn.
In 1831 Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction, the making of an electric current by moving a magnet near a wire. It was the basis of the generator and transformer.
Faraday's laws of electrolysis (1833-34) showed that the amount of substance deposited at an electrode is proportional to the electric charge passed through the solution.
James Clerk Maxwell's theory of the electromagnetic field (1865) showed that light is an electromagnetic wave, which unified the theories of electricity and light.

Werner von Siemens's self-excited dynamo (1866-67) made practical large-scale generation of electricity possible, but its benefits came mainly after 1871. The electric light bulb belongs to a later date.
notes.tip: Keep them apart: Faraday (induction 1831), Maxwell (field theory 1865), Siemens (dynamo 1866-67). Write 1866-67 for the dynamo, not 1866 alone.

notes.h: Electricity and communication: the telegraph and cables
notes.b: The electric telegraph used the new knowledge of electricity to send messages along wires faster than any messenger. This changed how news, trade and governments communicated.
points: William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented the British electric telegraph in 1837, and it was used on railways, on the Great Western Railway from 1838-39, where it helped signal trains.

Samuel Morse's telegraph was demonstrated in 1844 on a line between Washington and Baltimore, with the first message 'What hath God wrought'. Morse code, a system of dots and dashes, was widely adopted.

A submarine (undersea) telegraph cable was laid across the Atlantic in 1858 but failed within weeks. A lasting cable was completed in 1866, laid by the Great Eastern, so news and orders now crossed continents in minutes.
notes.tip: Keep Cooke and Wheatstone (British, 1837) apart from Morse (US, 1844), and the failed 1858 cable from the lasting one of 1866.

notes.h: Key personality: Charles Darwin
notes.b: Darwin was a naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection transformed biology. He was a witness to nature on his voyage and a careful theorist afterwards; most Christians in 1815 believed each species was created separately and the earth was young, which is why his theory caused such uproar.
points: Charles Darwin was born on 12 February 1809 at Shrewsbury. He studied medicine at Edinburgh (1825-27) and then at Cambridge (1828-31) to become a clergyman, and he was keenly interested in natural history.

He sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle (captain Robert FitzRoy) from December 1831 to October 1836, visiting South America, the Galapagos Islands (1835) and Australia. He collected fossils, rocks, plants and animals and noted variation between islands, such as finches, tortoises and mockingbirds.

Two books influenced him: Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830-33) showed an earth shaped slowly over vast time, and Thomas Malthus's essay on population (1798) described a struggle for existence.

Darwin kept notebooks on the transmutation (change) of species from 1837-38, worked on the theory from 1838 and published only in 1859. Alfred Russel Wallace's letter in 1858 pushed him on, and joint papers were read at the Linnean Society in London on 1 July 1858.

On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection (24 November 1859) argued from variation, the struggle for existence, natural selection (those best suited to their surroundings survive and breed) and common descent. The first printing sold out on publication.

The theory conflicted with the Genesis account and the idea of design. At the Oxford debate (30 June 1860) Thomas Henry Huxley defended Darwin against Bishop Samuel Wilberforce, who opposed him, and Darwin was absent.
notes.tip: Say he worked on the theory from 1838 and published only in 1859, not 'delayed twenty years'. Do not confuse Bishop Samuel Wilberforce (1860) with his father William Wilberforce, the anti-slavery campaigner.

notes.h: Key personality: Charles Darwin, controversy and legacy
notes.b: The Origin divided opinion, and Darwin let others fight in public while he wrote. Judgements of him changed from threat to founder of modern biology.
points: Huxley, known as 'Darwin's bulldog', Joseph Hooker and, eventually, Lyell supported him. Many churchmen and some scientists opposed him, though some Christians reconciled faith and evolution.
Describe the Oxford exchange without quotation marks for Wilberforce, because accounts of it differ and only appear in later sources.
The Descent of Man (1871) applied the theory to human evolution, the point critics found most offensive.
Darwin was a witness of nature on the voyage and a careful theorist. He took part in the debate through his books but avoided public controversy, leaving that to Huxley.

'Survival of the fittest' was Herbert Spencer's phrase (1864), which Darwin adopted in a later edition of the Origin, so he did not coin it. The misuse of his ideas as Social Darwinism was not his doing.

Darwin died on 19 April 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, which showed his standing. Historians regard him as the founder of modern evolutionary biology, and his theory was completed by genetics.
Contemporaries saw him as a threat to religion, attacked by churchmen and defended by Huxley, whereas later historians rank him among the greatest figures of the century.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level paragraphs earn marks for each correct dated statement: birth and education, the Beagle, the Galapagos, natural selection explained simply, the Origin (1859), Wallace, the Oxford debate, the Descent of Man and burial in Westminster Abbey.

notes.h: Biology: Pasteur, Mendel and the cell
notes.b: Biology moved from description towards explaining how living things work, with new ideas about microbes, inheritance and cells.
points: Louis Pasteur (1822-1895) showed from 1857 that fermentation and decay are caused by micro-organisms (living things too small to see without a microscope). This work led to the germ theory of disease, the idea that specific germs cause illness, which was established only in the 1860s-80s.

Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments, about 1859-62 (the early 1860s), showed that micro-organisms do not appear spontaneously in sterile broth, which undermined the theory of spontaneous generation (the belief that life arises from non-living matter).
Pasteur developed pasteurisation, heating liquids to kill microbes, in the 1860s.

Gregor Mendel (1822-1884), an Augustinian friar at Brno, published experiments on pea plants in 1866, showing that inheritance follows particular patterns. His work was ignored until its rediscovery in 1900, and Darwin never knew of it, so Mendel did not influence Darwin.

Cell theory: Matthias Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Theodor Schwann (animals, 1839) showed that living things are made of cells, and Rudolf Virchow's Cellular Pathology (1858) held that every cell comes from a cell.
notes.tip: Say Pasteur's work led to the germ theory, not that it developed it, and give his swan-neck experiments as the early 1860s. Separate Pasteur, Lister, Simpson and Snow.

notes.h: Medicine: anaesthesia and antiseptic surgery
notes.b: Before anaesthesia and antiseptics, surgery meant great pain and a high risk of infection. Two advances made operations bearable and safer.
points: Ether anaesthesia, which puts a patient to sleep so that surgery causes no pain, was demonstrated in Boston in 1846. James Young Simpson used chloroform in Edinburgh in 1847.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid in Glasgow in 1867, applying Pasteur's ideas about germs. Killing germs on instruments and wounds made surgery safer.
John Snow traced cholera to the Broad Street pump in London in 1854.
notes.tip: Keep the four apart: Pasteur (micro-organisms), Lister (antiseptic surgery), Simpson (chloroform) and Snow (cholera and water). Give short, dated statements of what each discovered and why it mattered.

notes.h: Technology: steam, railways, ships and photography
notes.b: Steam power and photography changed how people travelled, communicated and recorded the world, linking nations and empires in a faster network.
points: George Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill trials in 1829, and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830, so steam railways quickly became the model for others.
Isambard Kingdom Brunel's SS Great Britain was launched in 1843 with an iron hull and a screw propeller. The Suez Canal opened in 1869, shortening sea routes between Europe and the East.
Nicephore Niepce made the first surviving photograph about 1826, and Louis Daguerre's daguerreotype was announced in 1839.
William Henry Fox Talbot's calotype, a negative-positive process from which many prints could be made, was patented in 1841, so it could be copied where the daguerreotype could not.
Photographs were used for portraits and to record war and cities.
Henry Bessemer's converter (1856) made cheap steel possible.
Together, railways, the telegraph and steamships brought faster communication and travel, safer surgery and a new view of nature, and science challenged religious authority.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Niepce (first photograph, about 1826), Daguerre (daguerreotype, 1839) and Talbot (calotype, 1841). In science essays give each area at least two dated developments and explain their effect on society.

notes.h: Assessment: cultural, religious and scientific change
notes.b: Examiners reward judgement: what these developments achieved and where they fell short, and how contemporaries saw them compared with later historians.
points: Achievement: cultural nationalism gave nations symbols, languages and a shared past, and prepared the ground for political unity in Italy and Germany.
Limit: it reached mainly the educated minority, idealised the past and could not by itself win independence in Poland, the Czech lands or Hungary by 1871.
Achievement: the churches gave the poor charity, schools, temperance and moral reform, and renewed religion's role in public life.
Limit: the churches treated symptoms rather than causes, lost much of the urban working class, and in France were tied to conservatism.
Achievement: Faraday, Darwin, Pasteur and Mendel transformed knowledge, and technology such as railways and the telegraph changed daily life.
Limit: many benefits, such as electric power, germ theory in medicine and genetics, came only after 1871, and Darwin's ideas divided society.
Contemporary against later views: contemporaries saw Darwin as a threat to religion and Hugo as a controversial Romantic, but later historians rank both among the greatest figures of the century.
Overall: the period enriched national identities and expanded knowledge, but it also raised new questions about tradition, religion and national belonging that remained contested.
notes.tip: Always make the judgement explicit: strongest where there was no state, reaching the educated more than the masses, preparing rather than achieving unity. In France-is-unstable-but-cultural essays, state the agreement clearly.

keyTerms.definition: The cultural movement of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that celebrated emotion, imagination, the national past and the spirit of a people.
The idea, developed by Herder, of a national spirit expressed in a people's language, folklore and history.
The use of art, music, literature and language to express and create a sense of national identity.
The movement within the Church of England, begun by John Keble's 1833 sermon, that sought to restore Catholic elements to the Church.
Darwin's mechanism of evolution, in which individuals with variations suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully.
The theory, developed by Pasteur and others, that many diseases are caused by micro-organisms.
The principle, discovered by Faraday in 1831, that a changing magnetic field produces an electric current.
A system that sent messages along wires by electric current, developed in the 1830s and 1840s.
The belief that people sharing a language, culture and history form a nation that should have its own state, which artists, writers and musicians promoted in the nineteenth century.
The movement begun in 1848 by F. D. Maurice and Charles Kingsley to apply Christian principles to the problems of industrial society.
The French law of 1850 that gave the Catholic Church a large role in schooling by allowing church secondary schools and giving bishops seats on education councils.

factCards.definition: Johann Gottfried Herder developed the idea of a national spirit in the late eighteenth century, which nationalists later used.
Chopin's mazurkas and polonaises drew on Polish dance rhythms and became symbols of Polish national feeling in exile after 1831.
The opera Nabucco (1842) included the chorus Va, pensiero, which Italian audiences came to hear as a call for national liberation.
Liberty Leading the People, painted in 1830, shows a personification of liberty leading the crowd over the barricades.
The Brothers Grimm published Children's and Household Tales in 1812 and 1815, presenting German folklore as the voice of the people.
Manzoni's novel The Betrothed, set in Lombardy under Spanish rule, was published in 1827 and became a model for standard Italian prose.
Hernani, staged in 1830, caused a riot between Romantic supporters and classical critics, marking the victory of Romanticism in French theatre.
Victor Hugo's novel of 1862 portraying the poor of Paris and the revolutions of the nineteenth century.
Félicité de Lamennais founded the newspaper L'Avenir in 1830, arguing for the separation of Church and state and for freedom of the press.

factCards.term: Society of St Vincent de Paul, 1833
factCards.definition: Frédéric Ozanam founded this lay Catholic charity in 1833 to visit and help the poor and the sick in their homes.
Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836, collecting fossils, plants and animals in South America, the Galápagos Islands and Australia.
Darwin's book of November 1859 argued that species change over time through natural selection, and that all living things share common ancestors.
The 1860 debate at Oxford in which Bishop Samuel Wilberforce opposed Darwin's ideas and Thomas Henry Huxley defended them.
Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments, published in 1861, showed that micro-organisms do not appear spontaneously in sterile broth.
Gregor Mendel published his experiments on pea plants in 1866, showing patterns of inheritance that were ignored until 1900.
